title: Variables and types
description: Names, dynamic typing, and basic conversions
theory:
### Names and assignment

In Python, variables are **names** bound to objects. Assignment (`=`) attaches a
label to a value already sitting in memory rather than carving out a separately
managed memory slot by name alone. The same object can have multiple names, and rebinding
one name never magically changes another name unless you mutate a shared mutable
object through one of those names.

### What to internalize early

Use descriptive snake_case names. Use plain `=` for assignment; the walrus operator
(`:=`) belongs inside expressions (for example `if (n := len(items)) > 0:`). Constants-by-convention use
`SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` but remain mutable unless you freeze them (for example with
immutable types like `tuple` or `frozenset`).

```python
items = [1, 2, 3]
alias = items
alias.append(4)
assert items == [1, 2, 3, 4]  # same list object

x = y = []
x.append(1)
assert y == [1]
```

exercises.title: Declare a Variable
exercises.description: Declare a variable age of type int and assign it the value 25. Then use print to print it.
hints: After age = 25, call print(age) so the lone line renders as digits.

exercises.title: Multiple Variable Declaration
exercises.description: Declare two variables: name (string) with value "Pythonlang" and version (float) with value 1.21. Print them on the same line separated by a space.
hints: Assign name plus version exactly as spelled in the scaffold (literal string paired with fractional version).
print(name, version) emits both tokens separated by a single space.

exercises.title: Type Conversion
exercises.description: Declare an integer variable x with value 100. Convert it to a float and store in y. Print the result.
hints: Build y with float(x) before printing.
print(int(y)) keeps the emitted line numeric like the checker expects.

exercises.title: Zero Values
exercises.description: Declare variables of type int, float, string, and bool without assigning values. Print each one to see their zero values.
exercises.starter_code: # int_var, float_var, str_var, bool_var — use defaults, then print all four.
hints: Demonstrate builtins with print(0, 0.0, "", False) spaced like the canned answer.

exercises.title: Constants
exercises.description: Create a constant named MaxScore with value 100 and a constant named MinScore with value 0. Print both constants.
hints: ALL_CAPS bindings such as MAX_SCORE = 100 and MIN_SCORE = 0 model lesson constants.

exercises.title: Grouped Variable Declaration
exercises.description: Use a grouped var declaration to declare host (string, "localhost"), port (int, 8080), and debug (bool, true). Print all three values.
exercises.starter_code:
# host, port, debug = "localhost", 8080, True
# print(host, port, debug)
hints: Unpack host, port, debug = "localhost", 8080, True on one line.
print(host, port, debug) shows all three values.
exercises.solution:
host, port, debug = "localhost", 8080, True
print(host, port, debug)

exercises.title: Variable Swap
exercises.description: Declare two variables a and b with values 5 and 10. Swap their values without using a temp variable. Print the values after swapping.
hints: Simultaneous rebinding via a, b = b, a swaps without a temporary.
print(a, b) should read 10 5 separated by whitespace.
exercises.solution:
a, b = 5, 10
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
